text: Missus Monarch sat with a stillness that no professional could have equalled, yet, however I arranged her, she always came out the same, a tall, elegant figure who looked less like a character than like a photograph. <break time="0.8s" /> She was the real thing, but always the same thing, and I came to feel that her very perfection was a kind of prison from which no character in any story could escape. <break time="0.8s" /> The Major was no more useful, for, being six feet two and impossible to bend into any other shape, he could be employed only for the representation of brawny giants. <break time="0.8s" /> When I asked them to put on costumes, they would do so obediently, yet in a borrowed coat or a peasants shawl they somehow looked more like themselves than ever, the gentleman and lady stubbornly shining through. <break time="0.8s" /> Miss Churm, by contrast, could put on any role as easily as a hat, and the lady in my drawings, though Miss Churm was nothing of the kind, looked more like a lady than Missus Monarch ever did. <break time="0.8s" /> The truth, which I had always half known, now became painfully plain, namely that I had an innate preference for the represented subject over the real one, since the defect of the real one was so often a lack of representation. <break time="0.8s" /> Only then did I understand why my best ladies had always been drawn from a girl who was not a lady at all, for an artist needs not what is, but what can be imagined. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet I could not bring myself to send the Monarchs away, so patient were they, so eager to please, and so quietly anxious every morning when they climbed the stairs to my studio.
